cells.tense: Right now you're the one deciding what gets tended, and you're tending it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're tending and one thing it gives back — out loud, once.
cells.core:
You know what matters here before you can explain why. Two things need you at once and you're holding both without dropping either — not by force, by attention. You notice the quiet one before it goes under.

What you carry shows in how you show up: you tend the thing, you tend the people near it, and you keep the whole thing moving without making it about you. This kind of work closes sometimes — a season ends, something you were holding gets to be finished. Letting it finish is the next thing you're free to do, and it gives you back the room to tend what's growing now. So name what you're tending, and what it returns to you. One sentence, said once.

cells.tense: You're already living past this moment, bracing for the one where it all falls apart if you stop.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and do today's tending only — no plan past tomorrow — then stop.
cells.core:
What you give is real; the pace isn't. Two things need tending and you've started treating every moment as a chance to prove you can hold them both — checking, adjusting, staying a step ahead of a future that hasn't asked for you yet. That's not tending anymore. That's guarding, and it costs you the thing you're guarding.

Tending goes well when it's unforced: you give what's needed today and let tomorrow's needs arrive tomorrow. The way back is through the thing that satisfies without straining — what you've already made and felt, not what you might still have to hold. Pick one thing that needs you today, do that, and stop at the end of it. The part of you that knows what matters gets clearer when it's not scanning the distance every hour.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding the future instead of tending today.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: the part of you that knows what matters before it can say why

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already closed, while the things that need tending wait on the other side.
cells.ask: Choose one thing that's still growing, do one small act of tending for it today, then stop and let that be enough.
cells.core:
You can still feel which things matter — you know it in your gut — but you've gone quiet about tending them. Two things needing care became too heavy to pick up, so you set them down, and the setting-down has held. You didn't stop knowing. You stopped reaching.

The way back runs on what keeps going after everything else has stopped: strength that comes from still hoping. That's not a feeling to summon; it's an act done today. Choose one small thing that's still growing, do one tending for it — water it, check in, finish the piece you started — and let that be enough. What you're tending comes back to you slowly at first; the first act is the one that matters.
cells.sheetLine: You stepped back from tending, and it's still there to pick up.

cells.tense: You're tending what matters right now — the choice is running — and you talk about it as if it just happens on its own.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you tended this week and one thing it gave back, in your own words.
cells.core:
You know what to attend to — you're doing it — and at the same time it runs as if it were just the way things are. The care is yours; you're the one who notices the quiet thing before it goes under, and you decide where it goes. What you do is real. What's gone quiet is the credit.

When you tend well, you don't need a receipt — but the receipt is what makes the next season sayable: what you tended, what it gave back, what got to finish. Recognizing that isn't boasting; it's the honest accounting of what you gave, and it loosens the grip on holding it all silently. Write down one tending from this week and what it returned to you, in your own words. You may find the choice was yours the whole time.

attempts.check: The drafts risk implying I know what the person is trying to hold together or what they once lost. The reader could reasonably say: 'I'm not guarding a past — I just have two things I need to keep going.' The ask remains useful either way: naming what you're tending and what it gives back is true whether the read is right or wrong. The sentence I'd cut first is any that lets the writer sound like they know the person's history — I've kept those out.
